theory.title: Retrieving Data with SELECT, Aliases & Column Expressions
theory.summary: The SELECT statement is the fundamental command of SQL. It instructs the database engine which fields and expressions you want to project from a table.
theory.syntax:
SELECT column1, column2, (unit_price * 1.18) AS price_with_tax
FROM products;
explanation: A relational database organizes records into structured tables where columns represent attributes and rows represent records.
The FROM clause tells the database engine which table contains the source data.
The SELECT clause specifies exactly which attributes to project into the final result table.
Using SELECT * retrieves all columns, which is convenient for quick ad-hoc inspection but harms production performance by increasing I/O bandwidth and breaking covering index scans.
The AS keyword creates clean column aliases. Double quotes are required if the alias contains spaces, such as AS "Annual Salary".
Arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) can be evaluated directly within SELECT expressions without modifying the underlying database table.
The DISTINCT keyword removes duplicate rows across the selected combination of columns.
keyRules: SQL keywords (SELECT, FROM) are case-insensitive, but writing them in UPPERCASE is the industry convention.
Separate projected column expressions with a comma; never place a trailing comma before the FROM keyword.
Aliases defined in the SELECT clause cannot be referenced in the WHERE clause of the same query level because WHERE executes before SELECT.
Single quotes are reserved for string literals ('Sales'), while double quotes are used for identifier aliases ("Annual Pay").
commonMistakes: Missing commas between columns: `SELECT first_name last_name FROM emp;` treats last_name as an alias for first_name!
Placing a comma after the final column before FROM: `SELECT id, name, FROM emp;` triggers a syntax error.
Attempting to filter on an alias in WHERE: `WHERE annual_salary > 50000` fails because WHERE executes before SELECT.
Assuming SELECT evaluates first: While written first, SELECT evaluates after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING.
theory.exampleQuery:
SELECT product_name, unit_price, unit_price * 0.90 AS discounted_price, 'IN_STOCK' AS inventory_status
FROM products;
theory.exampleExplanation: This query retrieves the product name and base price, computes a 10% discount in a new column aliased as discounted_price, and appends a constant status column.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the SELECT clause in a SQL query?
options: To create and initialize a new table in the database
To specify which columns or expressions should be retrieved in the output
To filter out individual rows matching a condition
To arrange rows in ascending or descending sequence
questions.explanation: SELECT determines the column projection of the result set. Filtering is done by WHERE, sorting by ORDER BY, and table creation by CREATE TABLE.

questions.question: Why is using "SELECT *" considered bad practice in production application code?
options: It permanently deletes indexes on the queried table
It converts all numerical column values into plain text strings
It increases network I/O bandwidth, breaks index-only scans, and causes bugs if columns change
SQL-99 standards have completely deprecated the asterisk syntax
questions.explanation: SELECT * transfers unnecessary data across the network, degrades database buffer cache efficiency, prevents covering index usage, and risks schema mismatch errors.

questions.question: Given the query: SELECT first_name last_name FROM employees; what will the result contain?
options: Two columns: first_name and last_name
One column displaying first_name, aliased with the header "last_name"
A syntax error due to a missing comma
A concatenated single column merging both names
questions.explanation: Omitting a comma between two column identifiers causes SQL to treat the second identifier as an alias for the first column.

questions.question: Which of the following queries correctly calculates an annual salary from a monthly salary column and assigns a readable alias?
options: SELECT salary * 12 = annual_salary FROM employees;
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary FROM employees;
SELECT (salary * 12) TO annual_salary FROM employees;
SELECT RENAME(salary * 12, annual_salary) FROM employees;
questions.explanation: The "AS" keyword is the standard SQL syntax used to specify an alias for a projected column or computed expression.

questions.question: How must an alias be written if it contains spaces (e.g., Annual Salary)?
options: AS [Annual Salary] in all ANSI SQL engines
AS 'Annual Salary' using single quotes only
AS "Annual Salary" using double quotes
AS (Annual Salary) inside round brackets
questions.explanation: ANSI SQL standard uses double quotes for identifier names with spaces or special characters. Single quotes are reserved strictly for string literals.

questions.question: In the logical query processing order of an RDBMS, when does the SELECT clause execute?
options: First, before any other clause
Immediately after the WHERE clause but before GROUP BY
After FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING, but before ORDER BY and LIMIT
Last, after ORDER BY and LIMIT
questions.explanation: The database engine identifies the tables (FROM), filters rows (WHERE), groups them (GROUP BY/HAVING), and then projects requested columns (SELECT), followed by sorting (ORDER BY) and pagination (LIMIT).

questions.question: Why does the query: SELECT salary * 0.10 AS bonus FROM staff WHERE bonus > 500; fail in standard SQL?
options: Multiplication is not permitted inside the SELECT clause
The WHERE clause executes before the SELECT clause, so the alias "bonus" does not exist yet
Bonus is a reserved keyword in all relational database management systems
Decimal values must be enclosed in quotes
questions.explanation: Because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, aliases created in SELECT are not yet available to the WHERE filter.

questions.question: What does the DISTINCT keyword accomplish when placed immediately after SELECT?
options: Sorts all returned rows in ascending order automatically
Eliminates duplicate rows across all columns listed in the SELECT statement
Selects only the first row matching the query criteria
Enforces a unique constraint on the database table
questions.explanation: DISTINCT filters out duplicate tuples so that every row returned in the result set contains a unique combination of the selected columns.

questions.question: What will be the output of: SELECT 10 + 5 * 2 AS result;
options: NULL
questions.explanation: Standard operator precedence applies: multiplication (5 * 2 = 10) executes before addition (10 + 10 = 20).

questions.question: Which statement correctly retrieves distinct departments and job titles from the employees table?
options: SELECT DISTINCT department, DISTINCT job_title FROM employees;
SELECT DISTINCT department, job_title FROM employees;
SELECT (department, job_title) DISTINCT FROM employees;
SELECT UNIQUE department, job_title FROM employees;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT is written once after SELECT and applies to the entire combination of columns specified in the list.

questions.question: Which of the following is an invalid SQL SELECT statement?
options: SELECT id, name FROM users;
SELECT id, name, FROM users;
SELECT id FROM users;
SELECT 1, 2, 'active';
questions.explanation: A trailing comma after "name" right before the "FROM" clause violates SQL grammar rules and triggers a syntax error.

questions.question: What happens if you execute: SELECT 'Hello World' AS greeting; without a FROM clause in SQLite or PostgreSQL?
options: The query will crash because FROM is universally mandatory
It returns a single-row result table with one column named "greeting" containing "Hello World"
It creates a temporary table named greeting
It returns NULL
questions.explanation: Modern engines like SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL support selecting scalar constants and expressions without a FROM clause.

questions.question: If a table contains 10 rows and all 10 rows have the country "USA", what is the row count of: SELECT DISTINCT country FROM users;?
options: Error: Multiple duplicate values found
questions.explanation: DISTINCT consolidates identical values across the projection into a single unique instance: "USA".

questions.question: How do you select the product name and calculate an inventory value as (stock_qty * unit_cost)?
options: SELECT product_name, stock_qty * unit_cost AS inventory_value FROM products;
SELECT product_name, MULTIPLY(stock_qty, unit_cost) FROM products;
SELECT product_name AND stock_qty * unit_cost FROM products;
SELECT product_name, (stock_qty * unit_cost) INTO inventory_value FROM products;
questions.explanation: Standard arithmetic multiplication operator is "*", combined with AS for the column alias.

questions.question: Can you use the AS keyword to rename a table in the FROM clause?
options: No, AS is strictly reserved for columns in SELECT
Yes, you can alias tables (e.g., FROM employees AS e) to shorten table references
Only if the table has fewer than 100 rows
Only when executing DDL queries
questions.explanation: Table aliases are standard in SQL (e.g., `FROM employees AS e` or simply `FROM employees e`) to clarify and shorten column references.

questions.question: What is the result of selecting a NULL value with arithmetic, such as: SELECT 100 + NULL AS test_col;?
options: NULL
Throws a NullPointerException
questions.explanation: In SQL arithmetic, any operation involving NULL produces NULL because NULL represents an unknown value.

questions.question: Which query returns the employee ID plus an additional constant column called "status" with the value "Active" for every row?
options: SELECT emp_id, 'Active' AS status FROM employees;
SELECT emp_id, CONSTANT('Active') FROM employees;
SELECT emp_id WITH status = 'Active' FROM employees;
SELECT emp_id, ADD COLUMN status = 'Active' FROM employees;
questions.explanation: Literal values (numbers or quoted strings) can be directly projected as literal constant columns in SELECT.

questions.question: Are SQL keywords case-sensitive?
options: Yes, writing "select" in lowercase causes a syntax error
No, "SELECT", "select", and "Select" are syntactically identical to the engine
They are case-sensitive only in PostgreSQL
They are case-sensitive only on Linux servers
questions.explanation: SQL keywords are case-insensitive. However, convention mandates writing them in UPPERCASE for readability.

questions.question: What is the difference between single quotes ('') and double quotes ("") in standard SQL?
options: They are completely interchangeable
Single quotes enclose text/string literals; double quotes enclose database identifiers (column/table names)
Double quotes enclose strings; single quotes enclose comments
Single quotes are for numbers; double quotes are for characters
questions.explanation: ANSI SQL standard: Single quotes ('data') denote string literal values. Double quotes ("column name") denote database identifier names.

questions.question: Consider a query combining expressions: SELECT id, price, price * 0.9 AS discounted_price, 'PROMO' AS code FROM items; How many columns are in the output?
options: 2 columns
3 columns
4 columns
5 columns
questions.explanation: There are 4 comma-separated items: 1) id, 2) price, 3) price * 0.9 AS discounted_price, and 4) 'PROMO' AS code.

theory.title: Precision Filtering with WHERE & Operators
theory.summary: The WHERE clause extracts only rows that satisfy a specified criterion. Operators allow comparisons, range checks, pattern matches, and boolean combinations.
explanation: Comparison Operators: = (equal), != or <> (not equal), > (greater), < (less), >= (greater or equal), <= (less or equal).
Logical Operators: AND (both must be true), OR (either can be true), NOT (inverts truth value).
Text Operators: LIKE 'P%' matches anything starting with P; LIKE '_ublin' matches Dublin, Lublin (exactly one character prefix).
Range & Set Operators: BETWEEN x AND y is inclusive of boundaries (marks BETWEEN 40 AND 90). IN (v1, v2, v3) matches any listed value.
AND binds tighter than OR. Always wrap OR conditions in parentheses when mixed with AND!
keyRules: Single quotes ('...') are mandatory for text and date values; never use quotes for numeric values.
Wildcard % matches zero or more characters; wildcard _ matches exactly one character.
WHERE marks BETWEEN 40 AND 90 is equivalent to marks >= 40 AND marks <= 90.
commonMistakes: Writing WHERE dept = 'Tech' OR dept = 'Design' AND status = 'Active' without parentheses (AND will bind with Design only!).
Using double quotes for string values instead of single quotes.
theory.exampleExplanation: Returns cities with population between 500K and 5M whose name starts with B.

questions.question: What does the wildcard expression "LIKE '_ublin'" match?
options: Any word ending with ublin of any length
Words starting with exactly one character followed by "ublin" (e.g. Dublin, Lublin)
Only words that contain an underscore
All cities in Ireland
questions.explanation: The underscore (_) matches exactly one single character.

questions.question: What is the boolean result of: TRUE OR FALSE AND FALSE?
options: FALSE (because FALSE AND FALSE is evaluated first, then TRUE OR FALSE = TRUE? Wait!)
TRUE (AND has higher precedence: (FALSE AND FALSE) = FALSE, then TRUE OR FALSE = TRUE)
Syntax Error
NULL
questions.explanation: AND takes precedence over OR. So TRUE OR (FALSE AND FALSE) evaluates to TRUE OR FALSE = TRUE.

questions.question: Is BETWEEN 10 AND 20 inclusive of the number 10 and 20?
options: Yes, both 10 and 20 are included
No, only numbers from 11 to 19
Only 10 is included
Only 20 is included
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is always inclusive on both sides in SQL (>= 10 AND <= 20).

theory.title: Mastering NULL: Three-Valued Logic
theory.summary: In SQL, NULL is not a value; it is a marker for missing or unknown data. Standard arithmetic or equality tests against NULL yield UNKNOWN.
explanation: Three-Valued Logic: SQL booleans can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. If a WHERE condition evaluates to UNKNOWN, that row is NOT returned.
Equality check: `col = NULL` evaluates to UNKNOWN, never TRUE! Always use `col IS NULL` or `col IS NOT NULL`.
`COALESCE(val1, val2, ...)` returns the very first non-NULL argument. Perfect for defaults like `COALESCE(phone, 'N/A')`.
The NOT IN (NULL) Trap: If any row in a subquery contains NULL, `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT ...)` will return ZERO rows for the entire query! Always filter `WHERE id IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.
keyRules: NULL is never equal to anything — not even another NULL.
Aggregate functions (except COUNT(*)) completely ignore NULL rows.
In LeetCode problems (e.g. Find Customer Referee), always write: `referee_id != 2 OR referee_id IS NULL`.
commonMistakes: Writing `WHERE email = NULL` (will silently return 0 rows).
Assuming `referee_id != 2` includes people who have no referee (NULL is filtered out!).
Using NOT IN with a subquery that might return a NULL value.
theory.exampleExplanation: Returns customers with no referral_id and replaces NULL discounts with 0.

questions.question: What is the evaluation result of the expression: "NULL = NULL" in SQL?
options: TRUE
UNKNOWN
FALSE
Syntax Error
questions.explanation: In SQL, two unknown states cannot be proven equal. Hence NULL = NULL yields UNKNOWN.

questions.question: What does COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 50, 100) return?
options: NULL
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression from left to right (50).

questions.question: Why does "WHERE id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)" return zero rows for any row?
options: Because NOT IN checks "id != 1 AND id != 2 AND id != NULL", and anything != NULL is UNKNOWN, turning the whole AND expression UNKNOWN
Because NULL causes a fatal database crash
Because IN only accepts numbers
It is not zero rows, it returns all rows
questions.explanation: NOT IN expands to AND conditions. id != NULL is UNKNOWN, which kills the entire condition and returns no rows.

theory.title: Ordering & Limiting Results
theory.summary: In SQL, relational tables are sets of rows with NO inherent order. Unless you explicitly supply ORDER BY, the order of returned rows is undefined.
theory.syntax:
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table_name
ORDER BY column1 ASC, column2 DESC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;
explanation: ORDER BY sorts the finalized rows right before returning them to the client.
ASC sorts lowest to highest (A-Z, 1-100, earliest to latest date). It is the default.
DESC sorts highest to lowest (Z-A, 100-1, latest to earliest date).
You can order by multiple criteria: if the first column has ties, SQL uses the second column to break the tie.
LIMIT N restricts the result set to at most N rows.
OFFSET M skips the first M rows, making pagination simple: Page 2 with 10 items is "LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10".
keyRules: ORDER BY comes near the very end of your SQL query, right before LIMIT.
You can order by column names, column aliases defined in SELECT, or even expressions.
Never rely on the default order of a database table without an ORDER BY clause.
commonMistakes: Placing LIMIT before ORDER BY (syntax error: ORDER BY must precede LIMIT).
Assuming ORDER BY col1, col2 DESC makes col1 descending as well (col1 defaults to ASC!).
Using OFFSET without an explicit ORDER BY, which can cause inconsistent page results across requests.
theory.exampleQuery:
SELECT product_name, price, stock_quantity
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
theory.exampleExplanation: Returns the top 3 most expensive products in stock.

questions.question: What is the default sort direction when ORDER BY is specified without ASC or DESC?
options: DESC (highest first)
Random
ASC (lowest first)
The order rows were inserted
questions.explanation: ASC (ascending) is always the default order in SQL.

questions.question: In the clause "ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC", what happens when two employees have different departments?
options: They are sorted by salary first
They are sorted strictly by department name alphabetically
An error is raised
They are sorted randomly
questions.explanation: The primary sort is department. The secondary sort (salary DESC) only kicks in to break ties when employees share the exact same department.

questions.question: Which query retrieves the 2nd page of results with 10 records per page?
options: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 2
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10
PAGE 2 LIMIT 10
LIMIT 20
questions.explanation: Page 1 is rows 1-10 (OFFSET 0). Page 2 skips the first 10 rows (OFFSET 10) and takes 10 (LIMIT 10).

questions.question: Where must ORDER BY be placed in the sequence of SQL clauses?
options: Immediately after SELECT
Before WHERE
After WHERE (and GROUP BY/HAVING), before LIMIT
Anywhere in the query
questions.explanation: The clause structure is: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT.

theory.title: Text Transformation with SQL String Functions
theory.summary: Databases contain messy real-world text. SQL provides built-in scalar string functions to transform and clean strings directly inside queries.
theory.syntax:
SELECT 
  UPPER(name) AS uppercase_name,
  TRIM(name) AS clean_name,
  SUBSTRING(name, 1, 3) AS initials,
  LENGTH(name) AS char_count,
  REPLACE(name, 'a', '@') AS obfuscated
FROM students;
explanation: UPPER(str) / LOWER(str): Converts characters to uppercase or lowercase.
CONCAT(str1, str2, ...): Merges multiple strings into one.
SUBSTRING(str, start, length): Extracts a portion of text. Note: SQL uses 1-based indexing (start at 1, not 0!).
TRIM(str): Cleans leading and trailing whitespaces.
LENGTH(str): Returns the number of characters in a string.
REPLACE(str, from, to): Substitutes target patterns within a string.
keyRules: SQL substring indices start at index 1, NOT 0.
String functions return NULL if any required input string is NULL.
commonMistakes: Using 0 as the starting index for SUBSTRING (returns empty or first char depending on engine).
theory.exampleQuery:
SELECT first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name, UPPER(department) AS dept
FROM employees;
theory.exampleExplanation: Concatenates first and last name with a space and displays department in uppercase.

theory.title: Summarizing Data with Aggregates & GROUP BY
theory.summary: Aggregate functions compute a single summary value across a set of rows. GROUP BY breaks data into buckets before computing the summary.
theory.syntax:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS total_staff, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE is_active = 1
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY total_staff DESC;
explanation: COUNT(*) counts total rows including NULLs; COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is NOT NULL.
GROUP BY partitions the dataset into groups based on matching values in the specified columns.
The Golden Rule of GROUP BY: Every column in your SELECT clause must either be inside an aggregate function (e.g. SUM, AVG) OR listed explicitly in the GROUP BY clause.
WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping occurs.
HAVING filters groups AFTER grouping and aggregation have occurred.
keyRules: WHERE = row-level filter; HAVING = group-level filter.
Aggregate functions automatically ignore NULL values (except COUNT(*)).
Never write WHERE COUNT(*) > 2; always use HAVING COUNT(*) > 2.
commonMistakes: Selecting a raw column without including it in GROUP BY.
Attempting to filter on aggregate functions inside the WHERE clause.
theory.exampleQuery:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS average_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
theory.exampleExplanation: Groups employees by department, computes the headcount and average salary, and filters to only keep departments with at least 2 people.

questions.question: What is the crucial difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause?
options: There is no difference; they are aliases for each other
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups after grouping
HAVING filters individual rows; WHERE filters groups
HAVING can only be used on numerical columns
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before they are aggregated into groups. HAVING filters the summarized groups generated by GROUP BY.

questions.question: Why will this query produce an error in standard SQL? "SELECT department, first_name, AVG(salary) FROM staff GROUP BY department;"
options: AVG cannot be used with salary
first_name is neither aggregated nor included in the GROUP BY clause
GROUP BY requires at least two columns
There is no WHERE clause
questions.explanation: Any non-aggregated column in the SELECT list (like first_name) must be included in the GROUP BY clause.

questions.question: How do aggregate functions like AVG(salary) and SUM(bonus) handle NULL values?
options: They convert NULLs to 0 and calculate the average
They throw a database runtime exception
They silently ignore/skip NULL values in the computation
They make the final result NULL
questions.explanation: Standard SQL aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(column)) ignore NULL values when calculating results.

theory.title: Connecting Data with Joins
theory.summary: Relational databases normalize data into separate tables to eliminate redundancy. Joins allow you to reconstruct complete records across tables on the fly.
theory.syntax:
SELECT e.name, e.salary, d.dept_name, d.location
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d 
  ON e.dept_id = d.id;
explanation: INNER JOIN matches rows where the join condition evaluates to TRUE in both tables.
LEFT JOIN preserves EVERY row from the left table. If there is no corresponding record in the right table, the right table columns are filled with NULL.
The ON clause specifies the relationship condition, typically matching Foreign Key = Primary Key.
Self-joins allow comparing rows within the same table, e.g. finding employees who earn more than their managers.
keyRules: Always qualify columns that exist in multiple tables with their table alias (e.g. e.id vs d.id).
Be careful with LEFT JOIN when filtering in WHERE: putting a right-table column filter in WHERE turns it into an INNER JOIN.
commonMistakes: Ambiguous column name error when referencing columns present in both tables without an alias.
Missing join predicate resulting in accidental Cartesian products (CROSS JOIN).
theory.exampleExplanation: Returns all customers and their order history. Customers with no orders will still appear, with order columns set to NULL.

questions.question: If Table A has 10 rows and Table B has 5 rows, and you perform a LEFT JOIN from A to B, what is the MINIMUM number of rows in the result?
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN guarantees that every single row from Table A is preserved in the output. Therefore, the minimum number of rows is 10.

questions.question: You want to find all customers who have NEVER placed an order. What is the standard JOIN pattern?
options: INNER JOIN customers and orders WHERE orders.id = 0
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL
RIGHT JOIN customers and orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL
CROSS JOIN with COUNT(*) = 0
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all customers; for customers with no orders, the orders columns become NULL. Filtering WHERE o.id IS NULL isolates only non-ordering customers.

questions.question: What causes an "ambiguous column name" error in a JOIN query?
options: A column name is spelled incorrectly
Both joined tables contain a column with the exact same name, and you didn't specify which table it comes from (e.g., e.id vs d.id)
The column is of type VARCHAR
A table alias has spaces
questions.explanation: If both tables share a column name, you must qualify it with the table alias (e.g., e.id or d.name).

questions.question: What happens if you accidentally omit the "ON" condition in a JOIN?
options: The database throws an error or creates a Cartesian Product (every row of A paired with every row of B)
It defaults to joining on the first column
It returns an empty table
It joins on primary keys automatically
questions.explanation: Without a join predicate, the engine calculates a Cartesian product (CROSS JOIN), pairing every row of table A with every row of table B.

theory.title: Demystifying the SELF JOIN
theory.summary: A SELF JOIN is a regular join in which a table is joined with itself. It is indispensable for hierarchical structures (e.g., employee-to-manager) and pairwise comparisons.
explanation: A self-join treats the single physical table as if it were two separate tables with distinct aliases.

Alias 2 (`m`): represents the manager row.

keyRules: You MUST provide distinct table aliases for both instances of the table.
Use LEFT JOIN if you wish to retain the top boss who has `manager_id IS NULL`.
commonMistakes: Using the table name without aliases (raises duplicate table name in FROM error).
theory.exampleExplanation: Returns all employees and their managers, including the CEO whose manager is NULL.

questions.question: Why are table aliases strictly mandatory when performing a SELF JOIN?

Only for styling reasons

theory.title: Modular Logic with CTEs & Subqueries
theory.summary: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set defined before the main query using the WITH keyword.
theory.syntax:
WITH dept_averages AS (
  SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_dept_salary
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department
)
SELECT e.first_name, e.salary, d.avg_dept_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_averages d ON e.department = d.department
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_dept_salary;
explanation: Subqueries can exist in WHERE, SELECT, or FROM clauses.
Nested subqueries quickly become unreadable. CTEs solve this with readable, top-to-bottom steps.
A CTE is introduced with `WITH cte_name AS ( ... )` followed by the query that uses it.
You can chain multiple CTEs by separating them with a comma: `WITH cte1 AS (...), cte2 AS (...) SELECT ...`.
keyRules: The WITH keyword is written only ONCE at the start.
CTEs exist only for the scope of the single statement they precede.
commonMistakes: Writing `WITH` multiple times instead of separating with commas.
Putting a semicolon after the CTE definition before the main SELECT.
theory.exampleQuery:
WITH top_products AS (
  SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) as total_sold
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY product_id
  HAVING SUM(quantity) > 100
)
SELECT p.name, t.total_sold
FROM top_products t
JOIN products p ON t.product_id = p.id;
theory.exampleExplanation: Pre-aggregates total units sold into a CTE named top_products, then joins with product details.

questions.question: What is the primary readability advantage of CTEs over nested subqueries?
options: CTEs are read top-to-bottom like regular variables instead of inverted inside-out
CTEs bypass the SQL query parser entirely
CTEs permanently save tables to the hard drive
CTEs allow writing JavaScript inside SQL
questions.explanation: CTEs declare intermediate tables at the top of the query, making the logical pipeline clear and straightforward.

questions.question: How do you define multiple CTEs in a single query?
options: Write WITH cte1 AS (...), WITH cte2 AS (...)
Write WITH cte1 AS (...), cte2 AS (...) separated by commas with only one initial WITH keyword
Use the SUBQUERY keyword
Only one CTE is ever allowed per query
questions.explanation: You write WITH once, followed by comma-separated definitions: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ...

theory.title: Advanced Analytics with Window Functions
theory.summary: A window function performs a calculation across a set of table rows that are related to the current row, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does.
theory.syntax:
SELECT 
  employee_id,
  department,
  salary,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_salary_rank
FROM employees;
explanation: Unlike GROUP BY, window functions retain each original row while attaching the calculated analytic value.
PARTITION BY divides rows into groups/windows.
ROW_NUMBER(): Assigns 1, 2, 3... unconditionally.
DENSE_RANK(): Assigns same rank to ties with NO gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).
LAG(col, 1) OVER (ORDER BY date): Grabs the previous row's value.
keyRules: Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING.
To filter on a window function result, wrap it inside a CTE or subquery.
commonMistakes: Attempting to write `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() = 1` directly (must use CTE!).
theory.exampleExplanation: Finds the highest-paid employee(s) in each department, handling ties cleanly.

theory.title: Performance & Abstraction: Views & Indexes
theory.summary: Views provide simplified, secure virtual access to queries. Indexes provide fast pointer lookups (B-Tree) to avoid full-table scans.
theory.syntax:
-- Creating a View
CREATE VIEW high_earners_view AS
SELECT id, name, department, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 8000;

-- Creating an Index
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dept ON employees(department);
explanation: View: A saved SELECT statement that behaves like a table. A view does NOT store data itself (unless it is an indexed/materialized view); it executes the underlying query whenever called.
Why use Views: Encapsulates complex joins into a clean interface, restricts sensitive columns (e.g. hiding SSN/passwords), and standardizes calculations.
Index: An auxiliary data structure (typically a balanced B-Tree) that maps column values to row locations on disk, allowing logarithmic O(log N) lookups instead of O(N) full table scans.
Index Trade-offs: Reads (`SELECT WHERE col = val`) become dramatically faster, but Writes (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) become slightly slower because the index tree must be rebalanced.
SQL Command Families: DDL (Data Definition: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE), DML (Data Manipulation: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), DQL (Data Query: SELECT), TCL (Transaction: COMMIT, ROLLBACK).
keyRules: Do not over-index every column. Index columns that are frequently filtered in WHERE or joined in ON.
Primary keys are automatically indexed by relational databases.
commonMistakes: Assuming a standard VIEW duplicates and stores the underlying data (it is only a virtual query definition!).
theory.exampleExplanation: Creates a virtual view tech_leads and then queries it like a normal table.

questions.question: Does a standard SQL VIEW store duplicate copies of table data on the hard drive?
options: No, a view is a virtual table that executes its underlying query dynamically when accessed
Yes, it creates a physical copy of all rows
Only on Tuesdays
It stores data in RAM only
questions.explanation: Standard views do not store physical rows; they store the query definition.

questions.question: What is the main performance cost of adding an INDEX to a database table column?
options: Reads become slower
Writes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) become slightly slower because the index structure must be maintained
It deletes old rows
No cost at all
questions.explanation: Every write requires updating both the base table and the index tree structure.

hints: CREATE VIEW active_students AS SELECT id, name, marks FROM students WHERE is_active = 1; followed by SELECT * FROM active_students ORDER BY marks DESC;
